title: Victory, Revenge and a Golden Trap
overview: Gideon finishes off the Midianite army and takes harsh revenge, then turns down a crown but makes a gold object that leads Israel astray.

parts.label: Calming Ephraim's anger (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: The tribe of Ephraim, a proud rival of Gideon's own tribe, felt insulted at being left out of the first attack. Gideon calmed them by praising them, saying their "leftover grapes" (capturing two Midianite leaders) were worth more than his whole "harvest."

parts.label: Towns refuse bread (vv. 4-9)
parts.note: Sukkoth and Peniel, Israelite towns east of the Jordan River, refused food to Gideon's worn-out men, probably fearing Midianite revenge if he failed. Gideon swore to punish them once he had won.

parts.label: Capturing the two kings (vv. 10-12)
parts.note: The surviving Midianite army had fled far east. Gideon came by an unexpected desert route, caught them off guard, and captured their kings, Zebah and Zalmunna.

parts.label: Gideon's revenge (vv. 13-21)
parts.note: Gideon got the names of Sukkoth's 77 leaders and punished them with thorns, likely a brutal flogging, then tore down Peniel's tower and killed its men. He executed the two kings himself to avenge his brothers they had killed, and the text reports all this bluntly, without praising it.

parts.label: No crown, but an ephod (vv. 22-27)
parts.note: Gideon refused to found a royal family, saying the LORD alone would rule Israel, yet he collected about 1,700 shekels of gold from the plunder. He made it into an ephod, which here seems to be an object for seeking God's guidance, though scholars are unsure of its exact form, and people came to worship it, which trapped him and his family.

parts.label: Peace, then forgetting (vv. 28-35)
parts.note: Israel had forty years of peace, and Gideon had seventy sons plus Abimelek, whose name means "my father is king," an irony that sets up the next chapter. After Gideon died, Israel worshiped Baal-Berith, a local god whose name means "lord of the covenant," and forgot both the LORD and Gideon's family.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether to read Gideon mainly as a hero of faith, as the New Testament book of Hebrews lists him, or mainly as a warning, whose revenge and golden ephod show Israel's leaders sliding downhill.
think: Why do you think people who openly turn down power sometimes end up holding on to it in quieter ways?
